A secondary alcohol has –OH on a carbon bonded to two carbons: $R_2CH–OH$.
(I) $HOOC–N(CH_2CH_2OH)_2$: both alcohols are $–CH_2OH$ (primary); the –COOH –OH is not an alcohol. No $2^\circ$.
(II) $CH_3CH_2–CH(OH)–CH_2OH$: C‑2 is $2^\circ$. Yes.
(III) Ring C–OH is $3^\circ$; the side chain $–CH(OH)CH_3$ is $2^\circ$. Yes.
(IV) The side chain $HOCH_2–CH(OH)–$ and the ring CH(OH) are $2^\circ$. Yes.
(V) $CH_3CH_2C(OH)(CH_3)–CH(OH)CH_3$: the $CH(OH)CH_3$ carbon is $2^\circ$. Yes.
(VI) $(CH_3)_2C(OH)–C(CH_3)(OH)–CH_2OH$: two $3^\circ$ and one $1^\circ$ alcohol. No $2^\circ$.
Compounds with a $2^\circ$ alcohol: II, III, IV, V, so the total is 4.
Answer: (C) Four

Secondary alcohol: the carbon bearing –OH is bonded to exactly two carbons ($R_2CH\text{–}OH$).
(I) $HOOC\text{–}N(CH_2CH_2OH)_2$: both –OH are on $CH_2$ (primary); the –COOH OH is not an alcohol. No 2° alcohol.
(II) $CH_3CH_2CH(OH)CH_2OH$: C-2 is $CH(OH)$, a 2° alcohol. Yes.
(III) Ring C–OH is 3° (bonded to 3 carbons); side chain $CH(OH)CH_3$ is 2°. Yes.
(IV) Side chain $HOCH_2\text{–}CH(OH)\text{–}$ is 2°; ring $CH(OH)$ is 2°; ring $C(OH)CH_3$ is 3°. Yes.
(V) $CH_3CH_2C(OH)(CH_3)CH(OH)CH_3$: $CH(OH)CH_3$ is 2°. Yes.
(VI) $(CH_3)_2C(OH)\text{–}C(CH_3)(OH)\text{–}CH_2OH$: 3°, 3°, 1°. No 2° alcohol.
Compounds with a 2° alcohol: II, III, IV, V, which is 4.
Answer: (C) Four
